title: AI Disclosure — EPPS 6356 Assignment 4 (Chart Hackathon)
text:
Per the assignment rule “AI is allowed, with disclosure. For each chart, record the tool, model and version, date, and full prompts, plus two or three sentences on what you had to fix in the AI’s output.”
Each team member documents their own charts below.



Author: Shao-Kang (Eric) Huang Tool: Claude (Anthropic), model claude-opus-5, used in the Claude desktop app Date: 5 October 2026 Files produced: assignments/Chart4.R, R/theme.R, data/hpi_chart4_means.rds, output/chart4_continent_means.png


The conversation was held in Traditional Chinese. The prompts that produced the committed code are reproduced below with English translations.


接著幫我依照他的風格完成第四張圖 (Now complete the fourth chart for me, following her style.)

Context supplied to the model beforehand: the assignment PDF, the teammate’s published page https://nedretsencavus.github.io/portfolio/assignments/assign04.html, and read access to this repository after it was cloned locally — in particular assignments/Chart3.R, assignments/assign04.qmd, and data/hpi_clean.csv.

幫我看一下 (Take a look at this for me.) — sent with the first rendered PNG, which asked the model to review the output against the other three charts.






The y-axis title came out horizontal. theme_hackathon() re-declares axis.title.y through %+replace% without an angle, so the angle resets to 0, the title is printed flat at the far left, and the panel is squeezed. I caught this when I compared the first render against Chart 1, where the same fix (element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 2, margin = margin(r = 10))) already appears. The model had not carried that line over; it was added in commit 07f074f.
The first draft of the commit would have touched the whole repository. Because the clone is on a Windows machine, every text file in the repo showed as modified on line endings alone (13,521 insertions / 13,527 deletions across 52 files, all whitespace). I staged only the four new paths instead of using git add -A, so the commit history stays readable.
source("R/theme.R") pointed at a file that was not in the repository. Chart1.R and Chart3.R both call it, but the theme existed only inside the setup chunk of assign04.qmd, so those two scripts failed from a clean R session. I had the palettes and theme_hackathon() extracted into R/theme.R and verified that all four chart scripts now run from the project root, which is what the checklist item “code runs from a clean R session using only the repo contents” requires.





Sorting the continents by mean HPI rather than alphabetically, so the chart answers its own title.
Printing n = inside each column. Oceania’s mean rests on four countries and Asia’s on seventeen; without the counts the five columns read as equally reliable.
Stating the mean is unweighted in the subtitle, since Chart 1 uses a population-weighted mean and the two numbers would otherwise appear to disagree.






(Nedret: please add your tool, model, date, prompts and fixes here. If a chart was written without AI assistance, say so explicitly — the rule asks for disclosure either way.)



Tool: ChatGPT
Model: GPT-5.6 Sol
Date: October 6, 2026


Prompt 1:
“Help me redesign Chart 3 so that the Top 20 and Bottom 20 HPI countries are shown on one continuous horizontal scale rather than in separate panels. The redesign should improve direct comparison, remain consistent with the team’s shared theme and color palette, and still satisfy the assignment requirement of comparing one variable across many items.”
Prompt 2:
“Help me rework the Chart 3 code so that countries are ranked by HPI, Top 20 and Bottom 20 are distinguished with the shared color-blind-safe palette, exact HPI values are labeled directly, and the chart includes a data-driven takeaway title and a clear separator between the two groups.”
Prompt 3:
“Rewrite the Chart 3 implementation and analytical takeaway so that they accurately explain the redesigned continuous ranking, justify the visualization choices using comparison and perceptual clarity, and avoid making claims that are not directly supported by the chart.”



The initial AI-generated approach was revised to match the actual structure of the team repository, the shared theme.R file, and the variables available in hpi_chart3.rds. The final redesign replaced the earlier faceted layout with a single continuous ranked bar chart, used the project’s existing color-blind-safe palette, calculated the headline gap directly from the data, and adjusted file paths so the chart rendered correctly within the Quarto site. The analytical text was also revised to focus only on patterns directly supported by the visualization and dataset.

title: Chart Producing Hackathon: Visualizing the Happy Planet Index
text:
For Assignment 4 in Dr. Karl Ho’s EPPS 6356 Data Visualization course, our objective was to operationalize Andrew Abela’s Chart Thought-Starter taxonomy using empirical data from the 2024 Happy Planet Index (HPI). The assignment required building a fully reproducible, self-contained repository in R, deploying the resulting figures to GitHub Pages, and demonstrating clear collaborative ownership.
As team coordinator, I designed the foundation for the team before any visualization code was drafted. In line with Dr. Ho’s recommendation to settle design foundations early, I initialized the remote GitHub repository. I then developed, debugged, and refined Charts 1, 2, and 3, and established the branch architecture to delegate Chart 4 to my teammates.
This report documents the architectural setup, mathematical boundaries, visual design theories, debugging challenges, and substantive findings that went into completing this sprint. All figures share a unified styling system, adhere to Edward Tufte’s data-ink maximization, utilize color-blind safe palettes (Okabe & Ito 2008), and encode comparisons along common spatial baselines (Cleveland & McGill 1984).
## Visualization Engineering & Iteration


Load Dependencies, Theme, and Processed Datasets
pal_okabe_ito <- c(
  "orange"        = "#E69F00",
  "sky_blue"      = "#56B4E9",
  "bluish_green"  = "#009E73",
  "yellow"        = "#F0E442",
  "blue"          = "#0072B2",
  "vermilion"     = "#D55E00",
  "reddish_purple"= "#CC79A7",
  "dark_gray"     = "#333333"
)

pal_continent <- c(
  "Africa"   = "#E69F00", # Orange
  "Americas" = "#56B4E9", # Sky Blue
  "Asia"     = "#009E73", # Bluish Green
  "Europe"   = "#0072B2", # Blue
  "Oceania"  = "#CC79A7"  # Reddish Purple
)

pal_rank_comparison <- c(
  "Top 20"    = "#009E73", # Greenish (high wellbeing / sustainable efficiency)
  "Bottom 20" = "#D55E00"  # Vermilion (low wellbeing / high footprint)
)

scale_fill_continent <- function(...) {
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal_continent, ...)
}

scale_color_continent <- function(...) {
  scale_color_manual(values = pal_continent, ...)
}

scale_fill_hackathon <- function(values = pal_okabe_ito, ...) {
  scale_fill_manual(values = values, ...)
}

scale_color_hackathon <- function(values = pal_okabe_ito, ...) {
  scale_color_manual(values = values, ...)
}

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(forcats)
  library(scales)
  library(gt)
  library(gtExtras)
})


Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.5.2


Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.5.2


Warning: package 'gt' was built under R version 4.5.2


Warning: package 'gtExtras' was built under R version 4.5.2


Load Dependencies, Theme, and Processed Datasets
hpi_clean     <- readRDS("../data/hpi_clean.rds")
df_chart1     <- readRDS("../data/hpi_chart1.rds")
df_chart2_raw <- readRDS("../data/hpi_chart2.rds")
df_chart3_raw <- readRDS("../data/hpi_chart3.rds")



## Chart 1: Variable-Width Column Chart
### Implementation (Comparison: Two Variables per Item)
Chart 1 maps two continuous macro-demographic dimensions simultaneously using geom_rect(): continental population determines rectangle width (\(W_i = xmax_i - xmin_i\)), while population-weighted Happy Planet Index determines column height (\(ymax_i\)). Interior polygon text has been eliminated to maximize the data-ink ratio and prevent label clipping across narrower columns (e.g., Oceania).


Render Chart 1: geom_rect() Variable-Width Columns
theme_hackathon <- function(base_size = 11,
                            base_family = "sans",
                            axis_slant = FALSE,
                            legend_pos = "top") {
  
  th <- theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) %+replace%
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(
        size = rel(1.30),
        face = "bold",
        color = "#111111",
        hjust = 0,
        margin = margin(b = 6)
      ),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(
        size = rel(0.95),
        color = "#444444",
        hjust = 0,
        margin = margin(b = 12)
      ),
      plot.caption = element_text(
        size = rel(0.75),
        color = "#666666",
        hjust = 0,
        margin = margin(t = 12)
      ),
      
      axis.title.x = element_text(
        size = rel(0.90),
        face = "bold",
        color = "#222222",
        margin = margin(t = 8)
      ),
      axis.title.y = element_text(
        size = rel(0.90),
        face = "bold",
        color = "#222222",
        margin = margin(r = 8)
      ),
      axis.text = element_text(
        size = rel(0.82),
        color = "#333333"
      ),
      axis.line = element_line(
        color = "#777777",
        linewidth = 0.45
      ),
      axis.ticks = element_line(
        color = "#777777",
        linewidth = 0.40
      ),
      
      panel.grid.major = element_line(
        color = "#ECECEC",
        linewidth = 0.35
      ),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.background = element_rect(
        fill = "#FFFFFF",
        color = NA
      ),
      plot.background = element_rect(
        fill = "#FFFFFF",
        color = NA
      ),
      
      legend.position = legend_pos,
      legend.title = element_text(
        size = rel(0.85),
        face = "bold",
        color = "#222222"
      ),
      legend.text = element_text(
        size = rel(0.80),
        color = "#333333"
      ),
      legend.key = element_blank(),
      legend.background = element_blank(),
      
      strip.background = element_rect(
        fill = "#F2F4F8",
        color = NA
      ),
      strip.text = element_text(
        size = rel(0.88),
        face = "bold",
        color = "#222222",
        margin = margin(t = 4, b = 4)
      ),
      
      plot.margin = margin(t = 16, r = 18, b = 14, l = 16),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption.position = "plot"
    )
  
  if (isTRUE(axis_slant)) {
    th <- th + theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1)
    )
  }
  
  return(th)
}

p1 <- ggplot(df_chart1) +
  geom_rect(
    aes(
      xmin = xmin,
      xmax = xmax,
      ymin = 0,
      ymax = ymax,
      fill = continent
    ),
    color = "#FFFFFF",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      x = xcenter,
      y = ymax + 1.6,
      label = sprintf("%.1f", ymax)
    ),
    color = "#222222",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 3.4
  ) +
  scale_fill_continent(name = "Continent") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "Cumulative Global Population (Millions)",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02)),
    breaks = seq(0, 5000, by = 1000),
    labels = comma_format(suffix = "M")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Population-Weighted Mean HPI (Score: 0–100)",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
    limits = c(0, 75),
    breaks = seq(0, 70, by = 10)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "The Americas Deliver Highest Wellbeing Efficiency Despite Lower Demographic Scale",
    subtitle = "Width represents total continent population; Column height reflects population-weighted Happy Planet Index.",
    caption = "Source: Happy Planet Index (2024 Edition) & UN Population Division | EPPS 6356 Hackathon"
  ) +
  theme_hackathon(legend_pos = "top") +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_text(
      angle = 90,
      vjust = 2,
      margin = margin(r = 10)
    ),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(0.85)),
    legend.margin = margin(b = 4)
  )

p1












The Population Weighting Effect: Looking strictly at national averages, Latin American nations post the highest individual HPI scores globally. However, when weighting by population, Europe leads all continents with a score of 49.4 across roughly 750 million people. The Americas place second at 46.7; while countries like Costa Rica (62.1) and Colombia (60.2) demonstrate world-class efficiency, the region’s aggregate score is pulled down by the demographic mass and heavy ecological footprint of the United States (37.4 across 333 million people).
Demographic Mass vs. Sustainable Return: Asia spans the largest horizontal share of the chart—representing nearly 4 billion people in this sample—yet achieves an intermediate efficiency score of 44.9. Oceania maintains a solid 46.0, though its demographic footprint is a narrow sliver on the far right (roughly 32 million people). Africa records the lowest regional weighted score at 36.6 across roughly 880 million people, constrained primarily by systemic deficits in life expectancy and basic public health infrastructure rather than resource overconsumption.

title: Chart Producing Hackathon: Visualizing the Happy Planet Index
section: Chart 2: Table with Embedded Distribution Bars
text:
Chart 2: Table with Embedded Distribution Bars

Implementation (Comparison: Many Categories across Multiple Indicators)
Chart 2 presents 25 representative nations across development tiers. Built with gt and gtExtras, it embeds inline distribution bars directly into the data matrix, enabling pre-attentive length decoding along an aligned baseline while maintaining analytical precision.


Render Chart 2: gt + gtExtras Formatted Data Table
df_table <- df_chart2_raw %>%
  arrange(desc(hpi)) %>%
  mutate(
    footprint_bar = (footprint / max(footprint)) * 100,
    hpi_bar = hpi
  ) %>%

Analytical Takeaway

The Income–Footprint Decoupling: The inline pressure bars visually expose that high national wealth does not translate into sustainable efficiency. High-income economies like Luxembourg ($116,300 GDP pc) and Qatar ($93,500 GDP pc) achieve high life expectancy (82.6 and 79.3 years), but generate massive ecological footprints (12.80 and 14.30 gha/capita). These resource demands stretch their pressure bars to the maximum and drag their overall HPI scores down to 33.5 and 22.6.
High Efficiency at Low Cost: Middle- and low-income economies achieve comparable health and happiness outcomes at a fraction of the ecological throughput. Costa Rica ($20,300 GDP pc) and Vanuatu ($3,150 GDP pc) deliver life expectancies of 80.3 and 70.5 years with subjective wellbeing at 7.0/10, all while keeping footprints under 2.7 gha/capita. Their efficiency bars fill nearly two-thirds of the cell, demonstrating that human development does not require exponential carbon consumption.
Two Routes to Low Scores: The bottom rows highlight two distinct failure mechanisms. In the United States (HPI 37.4) and Qatar (HPI 22.6), low efficiency stems from excessive consumption (footprints of 7.80 and 14.30 gha). In the Central African Republic (HPI 21.1), the low score is driven by acute humanitarian hardship—life expectancy drops to 53.9 years and wellbeing falls to 3.5, even though its footprint is minimal at 1.45 gha/capita.

Chart 3: Horizontal Bar Chart of Ranked Cohorts

Implementation (Comparison: One Variable, Many Items)
Chart 3 compares the Top 20 and Bottom 20 HPI countries on one continuous horizontal scale. Countries are ordered by HPI using forcats::fct_reorder(), which removes alphabetical ordering and makes the ranking directly visible. Bar length and position encode HPI on a common baseline, while a color-blind-safe green–vermilion palette distinguishes the two cohorts. A separator line marks the boundary between the Top 20 and Bottom 20.

title: Chart Producing Hackathon: Visualizing the Happy Planet Index
text:
Analytical Takeaway

Large spread across the ranking: The continuous ordering reveals a substantial gap between the highest- and lowest-ranked countries. Costa Rica has the highest HPI score at 62.1, while the Central African Republic has the lowest score at 21.1, producing a difference of 41.0 points. Displaying all 40 countries on one common scale makes this overall spread immediately visible and easier to compare than if the two cohorts were shown in separate panels.
Regional concentration among the highest-ranked countries: Many of the highest HPI scores are concentrated in Latin America and the Caribbean. Costa Rica, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Jamaica, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Peru, Mexico, and the Dominican Republic all appear in the Top 20. However, the Top 20 is not regionally uniform, as countries such as Switzerland, Norway, Finland, Spain, Japan, Vietnam, and the Philippines also rank highly.
The Bottom 20 is geographically diverse: The lower end of the ranking includes countries from Africa, Europe, Asia, the Americas, and the Middle East. Examples include Senegal, Ghana, Kenya, Estonia, Bulgaria, Egypt, Uganda, the United States, Tanzania, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, South Africa, Sierra Leone, Mongolia, Zimbabwe, Qatar, and the Central African Republic. This indicates that low HPI scores are not confined to a single region.
The visualization emphasizes comparison rather than explanation: Chart 3 shows how countries differ in HPI score, but it does not by itself explain why those differences occur. Variables such as life expectancy, wellbeing, ecological footprint, and GDP per capita are present in the dataset, but they are not encoded in this chart. Therefore, the chart should be interpreted as a ranked comparison of HPI outcomes rather than as evidence of causal relationships.

text:
Technical Troubleshooting & Debugging Log
During development, several technical issues required hands-on troubleshooting to keep the project moving:

Package Installation & System Permissions: Running install.packages("dplyr", "tidyr", ...) initially threw directory errors because missing c() wrappers caused R to misinterpret package names as local paths and download repositories. In addition, Windows compilation prompts for Rtools appeared. I resolved this by setting options(pkgType = "binary") to pull pre-compiled binaries, avoiding unnecessary local compiler builds.
Quarto Path Resolution: Early preview runs failed with cannot open the connection on source("R/theme.R") because the file was saved in an external folder. I wrote an inline script generator to save R/theme.R directly into the project root, satisfying the self-contained repository requirement.
YAML Parser Crashes: Quarto threw readBlockMapping2 errors due to a merged title/subtitle line and non-breaking space characters (\u00A0) in the YAML header. I rebuilt the front matter with standard two-space indentation and dedicated lines for every key.
Table Cell Clipping: The gt table’s right-aligned currency columns were getting clipped during headless rendering in Chrome. Setting fixed pixel widths on every column via cols_width() resolved the overflow.

For all these errors I asked Gemini- Flash Extended model. I gave my code and the warning error I got in the console to Gemini and asked why it happpened, and how I could fix it.

title: About Me
text:
Hi! I’m Nedret Sen-Cavus, and this fall I’m in my second year of my Master of Science in Social Data Analytics and Research studies at The University of Texas at Dallas — the next step toward my dream of earning a PhD in Social Psychology and becoming a researcher–professor.
I’ve always been fascinated by how people think, feel, and act toward others — especially when group identities, social inequalities, and crisis situations are involved. My passion lies in understanding intergroup relations, social injustice, and how social identity shapes prosocial behavior.
I hold a B.A. in Psychology (Cum Laude) from Hacettepe University, and during my undergrad I spent six months at Radboud University in the Netherlands through the Erasmus+ exchange program, focusing on intergroup relations and prosocial/antisocial behavior.
I’ve also worked as a Graduate Research Assistant in Prof. Linda Tropp’s Intergroup Relations & Social Justice Lab at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where I helped design research projects, collect and analyze data (ANOVA, regression, correlations), and explore ways to promote social cohesion between diverse groups.
Beyond the academic details, I’m someone who:
Loves diving into books and new research articles
Thrives in collaborative, idea-driven environments
